deep.reconstruction:
The page has no mathematical derivations. It is a sequence of programmatic and philosophical notes on the foundations of mathematics, separated by horizontal rules. The notebook dates to about 1909-1910: the previous page cites Planck's 'Die Einheit des physikalischen Weltbildes' (1909) and 'Acht Vorlesungen über theoretische Physik' (1910), and says 'what we did as students 25 years ago'.

(1) Mathematics should engage with philosophy and logic as a counterweight to mathematics pursued for applications. It is a 'question of life' for mathematics: either it rules over both logic and the natural sciences, or it will be ruled.

(2) Logic and mathematics are 'an experimenting with thoughts and a thinking with mechanisms'. Experience and pure thought merge and border on each other there.

(3) The greatest progress often consists in turning an apparently absolute truth into a relative one.

(4) The axiom of choice, used with correct formal application of the writing rules, 'by means of experimenting' can never lead to contradiction. A mathematical experiment is one that cannot fail and is always certain, provided one pays attention. Paying attention means applying the rules correctly. Hilbert asks whether an 'Uebergeist' (a super-mind) is needed as a check.

(5) Proposed task ('Beweise, dass ...'). Show that if an ordinary statement S, for example of number theory or function theory, is found with the help of a general transfinite principle such as the axiom of choice, then S must also be directly provable without that principle. This is called 'elimination': passing from an indirect to a direct proof. Hilbert says this alone would give such transfinite principles a high value.

In modern terms: if T + AC proves S and S is 'ordinary' (arithmetical or similarly concrete), then T proves S. That is, AC is conservative over T for such statements. The previous page gives the companion relative-consistency claim: if a system of sets is consistent, it stays consistent when AC is added. Since T + AC proves S, if T did not prove not-S, adding AC would not create a contradiction. For a decidable (finitary) S this suggests T proves S. That is the familiar Hilbertian route from consistency to conservation. This interpretive gloss is mine; Hilbert gives no proof.

(6) A fragmentary remark: the most wonderful or remarkable thing is that mathematics is possible at all. Why is not every problem solved at once? The sentence continues on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors, since no proofs are given.
The claim that AC 'can never lead to contradiction' is asserted without proof. Relative consistency of AC was only established by Gödel (1938).

The conservation claim is stated as a task. Its full arithmetical form for ZF vs ZFC is a theorem (Gödel 1938 / Shoenfield absoluteness). For general 'function-theoretic' statements it is false without restricting their logical complexity.

results.what: Programmatic demand that theorems of number theory or function theory proved via transfinite principles (AC) be eliminable, i.e. directly provable without them.
results.modern_name: Conservativity of ideal/transfinite principles; elimination of ideal elements (AC conservative over ZF for arithmetical statements)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert's program (1920s: 'Neubegründung' 1922, 'Über das Unendliche' 1926). The ZFC/ZF arithmetical case was settled by Gödel (1938) and Shoenfield (1961).

results.what: View that AC, applied by formal rules, cannot yield contradiction, i.e. relative consistency of AC as the right formulation of the axiom.
results.modern_name: Relative consistency of the axiom of choice
results.usually_credited_to: Gödel 1938 (proof). Hilbert's early formulation in these notebooks is discussed by Peckhaus and Sieg.

results.what: Formal mathematics as 'experimenting on paper' with signs; logic as the place where empirical and pure thought meet.
results.modern_name: Formalist / finitist epistemology of proof theory

deep.surprise_reason: The elimination/conservativity idea is the core of Hilbert's later program and is well credited to him. Finding it stated explicitly for AC over number theory c. 1910 is a nice dated precursor. Historians (Peckhaus, Sieg) already know and quote the Cod. ms. 600 notebooks, so it is only moderately notable.
transcription_corrections: Line 5-6: probably 'entweder sie wird über beide, Logik und Naturwissenschaften, herrschen oder sie wird gewiss beherrscht'. The transcription's 'sie und also beide' looks like a misreading of 'sie wird über beide'.
The insertion '(mittels Experimentierens,)' is written below 'zum Widerspruch' and belongs after it: '... nie zum Widerspruch mittels Experimentierens führen'.
'Das Wunderbarste[?]' is perhaps 'Das Wunderlichste'. 'scheinen keine Lösung' is plausibly 'scheinbar keine Lösung'.
'In der That: das Merkwürdigste' has a semicolon after 'That' in the image, and 'Das' is overwritten as 'das'.
